solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: United correctly directed to hang on to apprentice

indicators.note: to hang on to something is to grip it, so the directing word holds the next piece within it

parts.note: led means guided or directed
APP is the short form of apprentice

explanation.surface: A football club, run properly, keeps hold of a young trainee.
explanation.walkthrough: United looks like a football club but is the definition: in joinery, two timbers lapped are properly joined by overlapping, hence 'correctly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapped is the carpenter's term for joined by a lap joint, where overlapping halves fit together.

clue.text: To Shakespeare's readers mean imperfect collection of texts

parts.note: lame means defective
the New Testament is a collection of texts

explanation.surface: A grumble that a set of texts is too poor for readers of Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mean' is the old verb meaning to moan; Shakespeare's readers would know it as to lament.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean, in its archaic sense, was to grieve or moan, a sense Shakespeare uses, matching lament as a verb.

clue.text: Reminiscence caught by clown to do with early notes?

parts.note: ana are collected anecdotes or reminiscences
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a clown in the old sense is a country bumpkin

explanation.surface: A memory captured by a jester involving some first jottings.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says 'caught by clown' but reads in order: memory, then the caught letter, then clown.
explanation.definitionFit: Anacrusis is an upbeat, unstressed notes before the first full bar, so anacrustic describes those opening notes.

clue.text: Traditionally Chinese resident, although in past

indicators.note: in sets the word for although inside the abbreviation for past

parts.note: pa is the dictionary abbreviation for past
and in archaic usage means even if or although

explanation.surface: Someone historically living in China, although that was long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda is native to China, a resident of its bamboo forests.

clue.text: En passant, I must cover worn-out foot

indicators.note: in a down entry covering means sitting on top, so the first pieces come above the last

parts.note: e.p. is the chess abbreviation for en passant
taken as written
trite means stale, worn out by overuse

explanation.surface: In passing, someone must bandage a tired foot.
explanation.walkthrough: Foot is the prosodic sense, a unit of metre.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitrite is a metrical foot of three long syllables and one short one.

clue.text: Rising Left on education in Sorbonne — not wanted

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means read upwards, so the letters go bottom to top

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
ED is short for education

explanation.surface: A left-wing educational movement rises in a Paris university, where it is unwelcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Sorbonne' tells you the answer is French, from the Paris university.
explanation.definitionFit: De trop is French for too much, used in English for someone whose presence is unwelcome.

clue.text: A swathe of academicians we regularly meet

indicators.note: a swathe is a strip cut out of something, so a run of letters is taken from the following words

parts.note: the run straddles the end of academicians, all of we and the start of regularly

explanation.surface: Some members of the Academy are people we see often.
explanation.walkthrough: Regularly looks like an instruction to take alternate letters, but it only supplies the final R of the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: To answer a need or purpose is to satisfy or fulfil it, the same sense as to meet it.

clue.text: Whiffs when circling Urbs Aeterna, as they call it

indicators.note: circling means going round, so the word for when encloses the city name

parts.note: as means when, at the time that

parts.words: Urbs Aeterna, as they call it
parts.note: the Eternal City in its own Italian name

explanation.surface: Smells noticed while touring the Eternal City, using the locals' name for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiffs are faint smells, and aromas are smells, usually pleasant ones.

clue.text: Quiet cut means an indistinct sound

indicators.note: cut means trimmed, so the final letter is lopped off

parts.note: sh is a call for quiet
a way is a means or method

explanation.surface: Quiet, reduced methods produce a muffled noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Shwa, or schwa, is the neutral unstressed vowel, as in the first syllable of about.

clue.text: Very special fish in outer limits?

parts.note: way means very, as in way too much
S is short for special
ides are freshwater fish, the plural of ide

explanation.surface: Remarkable fish found at the furthest edges.
explanation.walkthrough: Fish looks singular but can be plural, giving the plural of a crossword fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Waysides are the edges of a road, its outer limits in a playful sense, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Roller in which army corps must replace head to drive again

indicators.note: replacing the head means swapping the first letter for something else

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a roller is a large wave, as is a surge

explanation.surface: A wave in which soldiers take the lead to push forward once more.
explanation.definitionFit: To urge is to drive or press on, so reurge means to drive or press again.

clue.text: Academician and a college in step for investigation

indicators.note: in places the earlier pieces inside the word for step

parts.note: a phase is a stage or step in a process
A is a Chambers abbreviation for academician, as in ARA
as in five pounds a day, i.e. per day
C is the standard abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: An academic and a college moving in unison, apparently for some inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is only a joining word; 'a' is the piece that becomes PER.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper chase is a laborious search through documents, a bureaucratic kind of investigation.

clue.text: Sweet alcohol mixed in malt, no?

indicators.note: mixed suggests ingredients stirred together and their order lost

parts.note: the fodder letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about whether a sweet spirit is blended into malt whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Mannitol is a sugar alcohol with a sweet taste, used as a sweetener and in medicine.

clue.text: Gentle weeping two bishops expressed for one quite unlike Jack

indicators.note: expressed here means squeezed out, so letters are pressed out of the words

parts.note: bland means mild or gentle
to blubber is to weep noisily
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: Soft crying from two clergymen for someone very different from Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack is a Jack tar, a sailor; the two outer Bs go from the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlubber is someone unused to the sea, the opposite of a Jack tar, a seasoned sailor.

clue.text: English chap's gentle oath, one that's dated

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
cod is an old slang word for a fellow or chap

explanation.surface: An Englishman's mild expletive, now rather old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecod is an archaic mild exclamation, a minced form of 'by God'.

clue.text: Great potentate accepting a fawn, silky garment

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the ruler's title receives the article

parts.note: a tsar was the Russian emperor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mighty ruler receives a young deer and a silken robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fawn' looks like a baby deer being accepted; it is the colour, part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasar, or tussore, is a coarse fawn-coloured silk, so the word names both the colour and the fabric.

clue.text: Take in routine beast, one shining brightly

indicators.note: in places the recipe abbreviation inside the word for routine

parts.note: a comedian's act is a routine
R, from Latin recipe, means take on prescriptions
the urus is the extinct wild ox, or aurochs

explanation.surface: Incorporate a routine involving an animal that dazzles.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern sky, a red giant in Boötes.

clue.text: Curtailed tour with a rip-off rocket

indicators.note: curtailed means having its tail cut, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a band on tour is on the road
a sting is a swindle

explanation.surface: A shortened trip accompanied by a con involving a rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: Rocket looks like a firework or space vehicle; in British slang a rocket is a severe telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: A roasting and a rocket are both informal British words for a stern reprimand.

clue.text: One who supplies articles could be smart one

indicators.note: could be means might be turned into, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer who supplies newspaper pieces might be a clever person.
explanation.walkthrough: Articles look like newspaper pieces but are goods handed out from stock.
explanation.definitionFit: A storeman looks after a stockroom and issues goods, items or articles, to those who need them.

clue.text: Watch performer cutting remark when Queen's absent

parts.note: a turn is a performer or act in a variety show

indicators.note: absent means missing, so the royal abbreviation is removed

parts.note: a quip is a sharp or witty remark
Qu is an abbreviation for queen

explanation.surface: Watch an entertainer make a barbed comment when the monarch is out of the room.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnip was slang for a large, thick old-fashioned pocket watch.

clue.text: Extraordinary deeds surrounding tense case in the old days

indicators.note: surrounding means enclosing, so the rearranged letters go round the grammar abbreviation
extraordinary means out of the ordinary, so the letters are not in their usual order

parts.note: fodder taken as written
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Remarkable exploits surrounded a tense legal case in times past.
explanation.definitionFit: Stedde is an obsolete spelling of stead, a place or situation, hence case in old usage.

clue.text: In Hamlet, maintains squires wanting resistance

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: to squire a lady is to escort her
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: In the play, someone keeps attendants but they lack staying power.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet the players are said to be 'escoted', meaning paid for and maintained.
explanation.definitionFit: Escot is an archaic Shakespearean verb meaning to pay for or support, hence maintains.

clue.text: Having scored better than most ditch Scottish kite

parts.note: ea is a dialect word for a drainage channel in the Fens
gled is a Scots and northern word for the kite

explanation.surface: Someone who outscored most people gets rid of a bird from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Ditch looks like a verb, to get rid of; it is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf an eagle is two strokes under par on a hole, a score better than most players manage.

clue.text: Finding nothing in ground round British Library swear

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the word for ground encloses the other pieces

parts.note: sod is turf, the ground
BL is the abbreviation for the British Library
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: Discovering nothing in the grounds of the national library makes one curse.
explanation.walkthrough: Swear is a noun here, an oath, as in informal 'swear word'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Sblood, from God's blood, is an archaic oath, so the answer is a swear word.

clue.text: First flivver off assembly line in Delaware in shed there

indicators.note: in places the state abbreviation inside the word for shed

parts.note: molt is the American spelling of moult, 'there' pointing to America where Delaware is
DE is the postal abbreviation for Delaware

explanation.surface: The first cheap car off a production line is housed in a Delaware garage.
explanation.walkthrough: A flivver is old American slang for a cheap car; Ford's Model T was the first car built on a moving assembly line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ford Model T was the archetypal flivver and the first car mass-produced on an assembly line.

clue.text: Spoil mostly meagre Maori seafood

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to mar is to spoil
arid means barren or meagre

explanation.surface: Ruin most of a scant traditional New Zealand fish dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Marari is a New Zealand fish, the butterfish, eaten by Maori.

clue.text: Extremely artificial tree

parts.note: too means excessively
art means artifice, the opposite of nature

explanation.surface: A tree that looks very fake.
explanation.definitionFit: Tooart, usually spelt tuart, is a Western Australian eucalyptus, a timber tree.

clue.text: Where to get them in in practice?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: where you order a round of drinks
second meaning: practising as a barrister

explanation.walkthrough: 'get them in' is British for buying a round of drinks; a barrister is called to the Bar and practises there.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both standing at a pub counter and working as a practising barrister in the courts.

clue.text: Wife warmed up small appetisers

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
het, as in het up, is dialect for heated
S is the clothing abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A spouse reheated some little starters.
explanation.walkthrough: Appetisers look like starters, but here it means things that sharpen appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: A whet is something that sharpens the appetite, such as a small drink before a meal.

clue.text: One in wind to tilt, per Spenser

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the word for wind

parts.note: a gust is a blast of wind
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone out in a gale tries to lean over, as the Elizabethan poet puts it.
explanation.definitionFit: Giust is Spenser's spelling of joust, and to tilt is to joust with lances.

clue.text: Pet to lurk wanting what comes second

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, and what comes second points to the letter in position two

parts.note: to skulk is to lurk furtively

explanation.surface: An animal that likes to hide is missing out on its share.
explanation.walkthrough: Pet looks like an animal, but a pet is a fit of bad temper.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a pet is to be in a sulk, a fit of peevish ill humour.

clue.text: Clownish sort of dingbat

parts.note: a hob is a rustic or clownish fellow
O is a short form of of, as in o'clock

explanation.surface: A buffoonish type of oddball.
explanation.walkthrough: Dingbat looks like a fool, matching 'clownish', but here it is Australian slang for a tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang a dingbat can be a tramp or vagrant, which is what a hobo is.

clue.text: Repeatedly return from work at morning place of seclusion?

parts.note: to do is to work or perform
a.m. means morning
Napoleon's island of exile

explanation.surface: Someone keeps coming back from the office to a morning retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: The singer Nellie Melba gave so many 'farewell' performances that her name became a byword for comebacks.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a Melba is to keep coming out of retirement after announcing a farewell, an idiom from the soprano.

clue.text: Clear of particles? Cleared out parts

indicators.note: parts as a verb means separates, so the letters are broken up and regrouped

parts.note: the fodder letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about clearing particles, answered by an emptied-out space.
explanation.definitionFit: To edulcorate is to purify by washing away soluble or gritty matter, chemist's language for freeing of impurities.

clue.text: Harrowed Hell being close to parasite?

parts.note: Dis is the Roman underworld
a ked is a sheep tick

explanation.surface: Tormented by hell and pressed up against a bloodsucker.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrowed looks like distressed, fitting hell, but it is the farming sense: worked with a disc harrow.
explanation.definitionFit: To disk land is to cultivate it with a disc harrow, so disked and harrowed are farming synonyms.

clue.text: Supplement, say, still stocking section

indicators.note: stocking means holding in stock, so the word for still contains the abbreviation

parts.note: inert means motionless
S is the abbreviation for section

explanation.surface: An extra sheet, perhaps, still found within a section.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's supplement is one example of an insert, a loose item placed inside.
